sections.overview: Agriopis marginaria is a geometrid moth that appears unusually early in the year, with males flying in late winter and early spring. Its ochre to pale yellow-brown wings carry a distinctive broken, dotted border, while the female is flightless and has only tiny vestigial wings. The caterpillars feed on a range of deciduous trees and shrubs. Because the male's published wingspan varies considerably among regional references, measurements should be tied to their source and population rather than treated as a single fixed value.
sections.identification: Male wingspan is given as 27–32 mm by UKMoths and 36–42 mm by Hantsmoths; these regional accounts disagree, so the figures are best retained as source-specific estimates. Females are flightless with strongly reduced, vestigial wings and a larger-bodied appearance; no reliable body length, mass, body height or width, or sex-specific mass comparison was found. Male forewings range from pale yellow or ochre to rusty brown and may be heavily darkened; a broken row of dark dots along the outer border is a useful clue. The female's reduced wings distinguish her from flying females of similar winter moths. Males can be confused with the related Scarce Umber (Agriopis aurantiaria) and Mottled Umber (Erannis defoliaria); compare the wing shape, colour and border markings rather than relying on season alone.
sections.habitat: It occurs in deciduous woodland, scrub, hedgerows, gardens, heathland and other places where broad-leaved host plants grow. European sources document it widely, while British records describe it as common in suitable woodland and bushy habitats. Adults emerge during the cold part of the year, so mild weather can bring the first males out as early as mid-winter in some Central European localities; the main British flight is February to April.
sections.diet: The caterpillars are polyphagous on deciduous trees and shrubs. Regional records list oaks, hawthorn, blackthorn, birches, hazel, willow, elm, sycamore, apple and plum, among others. This broad host range is consistent with the moth's occurrence in mixed woodland, orchards, hedges and gardens; the adult diet was not documented in the sources reviewed.
sections.behavior: Males fly at night and are attracted to lights, even in cold weather; females cannot fly and climb tree trunks to release pheromones and attract males. This marked difference between the sexes is a distinctive part of the species' winter activity. The caterpillar's resting posture and colour can make it resemble a small twig, reducing visibility on host branches.
sections.reproduction: Adults appear mainly from February through April in Britain, with earlier records possible in mild Central European winters. After mating, the flightless female lays eggs on host trees; the larvae feed on deciduous foliage and the species passes the summer and autumn as a pupa before adults emerge in winter. Sources agree on the winter-to-spring adult period but provide limited consistent detail on clutch size and exact egg placement.
sections.ecology: Its larvae are part of the foliage-feeding insect community of temperate deciduous woods and hedgerows, and can serve as prey for birds and other insectivores. The moth's winter flight brings adult activity into a season when few other larger moths are on the wing. It uses numerous common native trees and shrubs, so its persistence depends on retaining structurally varied woody habitats rather than a single host species.
sections.conservation: Regional British moth accounts describe Agriopis marginaria as common and widespread in suitable woodland, scrub and hedgerow habitats. No global conservation assessment or range-wide population trend was found in the sources reviewed, so British abundance should not be applied to every part of its European range. Maintaining mixed deciduous woodland, hedges and native shrubs preserves the varied larval food plants on which it depends.
